They ere fed with milk, boiled Been, and water. lo their wild state they are Very destructive to birds, poultry, and young rebbits and are great deveurere of egge. There is no wonder at " Nemo" being pumled about tie Egyptian years. The Egyptians confounded the reeolutions of the he.venly bodies with the reigns ol their most eaelY monarch.. Hence the incredible number of years in tbe ' reigns of their eight superior gods„ who, according to them, dlled the Egyptian throne titilMeniaelv in the most early periods of time. To them, according to- their system, me. ceeded twelve demigod., who likewiae reigned an amazing number of years. These imaginary reigns ware merely the periodical revolutions of the heavenly bodies. Fleece the fabulous antiquity of that kingdom. The imaginary exploits and adventures of these gods and demigods furni.hed On inexhaustible fund of mythological romance& To the demi- gods succeeded the kings of the cynic cycle, personages equally chimnical with the former. After these prMees came another 'ace, denominated Nekyes. a title implying royal, splendkt, glorious. Them cycles figure high in the mythological annals of Egypt, ,and flan, furnished materiale for a vanety of learned disquisitions. The years and adven• three of Osiris, Orus, Typhon, and other allegorical person- ages ; the wandering. of Isis, the traneformationo of the gods into various animals ; their birth. education, peregrine- lions. and exploits—coronose a b .dy of mythological fictions on complicated, in ridiculous, and often so abound, that all attempt. to explain them have hitherto proved saeuceese- NI. All those extravag-ant fables are the offspring of hieroglyphical or allegorical emhtema, devised by the priests and sages of that nation, to conceal the mysteriea Of their ' religion from the inferior rooks. E. JORSIMOS, Runcorn.

Lent Sunday was a day of disaster in several par. of Switserland. fly the upeettion of a boat near Ottehy two perwns were drowned in the Lake of Geneva; five persons !oat their lives by a dre at Muti ;and Egg, in Berne, end the commun. of Hahn..., Frutigen, nod severalethern in the same canton were devastated bye terrible thunder and bud storm. The are is supposed to her. been the work of an incendiary, and it was with great difficulty that the man who is ...peered of having cotrunitted the crime WM pro- tected from the vengeance of the villager.. Nearly every bridge about Frutigon was carried away by the Morro, the roads are broken up, and the peasants and agriculturirds of the neighbourhood are all kelt ruined by the damage done to their buildings and land. On Monday morning the moun- tain pastures were still thickly covered with hailstones, end the vAlleys were so deeply flooded that they had the Appear- ance of 114 hes. _ ......

Detailed ac:;ot;bis—rec-eri-ved by the Wee India mail steamer show that the hurricane on August II was one of the moat deetructive within living memory. The churCbee and chapel. of Kingston were all partially destroyed. ;den the wharves and shipping. The colonial secreta,y's office was gutted, and the documents scattered. Private houses innumerable were utterly destroyed, and the Royal NaVli Club was wrecked, the seas washing clean over it. The homelese person. were sheltered in the Government dock- yard, which was lese injured. The Ihovernmant telegraph cfli.-re was deetroyeal, and its occupants blown long dmtances. Distrees was apprehended as the result of the damage.

A ElcxnartraN OATH Casa—A student of Hungarian Parliamentary history informs the Pester Lloyd that a case reaembling the Bradlaugh incident occurred in the Hungarian Diet in the year 1729. Two Protestant deputies who were appointed members of a finance committee refused to take the usual oath because it contained a reference to the Virgin Mary, giplich they conscientiously objected. Thereupon they were excluded from the deliberations of the committee, and prweedings were commenced against them in the Diet for contumacy. But the then Emperor of Germlny,Cliarles VI. (King Charles 111. of Hungary), father of the Emprees Maria Theresa, calmed the rng excitement, and solved the difficulty by an Act of sovereign prerogative, and exempted the Proteetant deputies from reeitidg in the oath the clause referring to the Virgin Mary. Pere Moinets with the Tan- ganyika detachment, had arrived stately at the Lzike, after experiencing sericite difficulties on the road, whieh, indeed, they would probably not have been able to overcome but for the timely succour received front the Belgian station at Karema. At the date of the last letters there rear no certain intelligence of the party destined for the Victoria Nyanza, which was under Pere Levesque, and had parted company with the Tanganyika detachment, probably at Tahoe,. It wis rumoured, however, on native authority, that they had hod a severe encounter with natives on the road, owing to one of their escort, an en-Cocoon, having killed amen. It is quite possible that the true explanation may be that they intd been attacked by bandits. The original expedition at Lake Tanganyika, under Pere DeniataL is said to be in a ; satisfactory condition, and to have established s•veral sta-; tions on the lake-shore. Theme.. few men of middle age, enjoying the mat solowit health, who would impose upon themselves a pedestrian feat such ae that which the septegmarian Premier performed on Monday evening to reach his well-known castle of Hawarden on the Flintehire hill. Starting by train on Monday afternoon, company with Mrs. Gladstone, from Mentmore, Backs, where the diatinguished maple had been making a brief stay with the Earl and Counter, of B,oseberry, the Premier arrived at Chester at twenty- five minutes past seven o'clock in the evening, and, in company with his commit, paid a visit to Dr. Jacob- -11011, the Bishop of Cheater. Leaving Mrs. Gladstone to follow by train, the Premier started ofi through the Bishop's garden, along the beaks of the Do., poet the old City Walls, nod on to the Hawarden• road, and then walked eight miles across the country to Mawarclen Castle, which he reached soon after ten . o'clock. Drum Or A RrnroMur Woßmr.—On Mon- day, an mquest wt. held at the Duke of Wellington public- house, Percivare-Inne, Runcorn, before Mr. Ridgwey, county coroner, on the body of Jane Hall, the wife of John Hall, waterman, who died suddenly on the previoas Friday. —Frances Hall, the daughter of the deceased, said bar 1 mother was 57 year of age. On the previa]. Thur.dav ! night deceaeed oleo with her, and on the 10th inst. she (wit- nese) got up about dye minutes to six in the morning for the purpose of going to her work, leaving her mother in hes. Lkeceased had complained of a pain in ber side, and had been eubject to a sore throat. She bad been accustomed to take a little drink, and had had a little on Thursday night.— Mare Buckley, • neighbour, said deceased bad complained of pains In her aide and throat, but only after ehe bed been drinking. On Friday morning, she called at deceased'e, I about hall,past eleven, and, not seeing her, she and a Mr. Cooke went upstairs and found her In her bedroom sitting in in her chair, leaning her head upon the tgble quite dead and cokl.—Dr. McDougall said he had made a post marg.. ex- amination of decestek, whose death had resulted front fail- ure of the heart's action. From her condition, he Judged that she had not taken much food or nourishment for some- thing liken fortnight. People who took drink eornetimes partook of very little food, for the appetite beumedestroyed, and all the craving was for drink. The liver would weigh about 121 k.. or 14k.., It, ordinary weight being about 4 1b.., and this would be brought on by drinking beer. —The Jury, After some deliberation In private, returned a verdict of a Died fro 22 disease of the heart.:

ROWOORN NATURatlell' Ffacn Cf.ol.—The last field• day for the union IND was held on Saturday last at lielsby. A small though veer select party of ynung people met and proceeded from Runcorn Motion, at two o'clock, for the day's work, amongst the boulders of Helshy Cliff. From the station they worked their way along the central walk on the face of the hill, where they enjoyed a noble prospect, and it wee made much more enjoyable by • brief deuriptlon of the geological formation, with the water St.., and the glacial drift, given by the secretary, Mr. !Northing, aided by Mr. Hargreaves, the chemist, of Widnes. Afterwards the walk erns continued upwards until the party found themadve• at Armour'. Lake, a large mere at the eummit of the hills. Here were toned several autumnal wild flower., vie., Golden Rod (Solidago Ifiu-aurea), Yellow Snapdragon (Linaria volgaris). This plant, pointed out by one of the ladies, is generally known as Butter-and- Edge, by the Cheshire peasantry. Why it is no named there, onginated • very animated discussion by the member, of the club. Avery witty gentleman magemed the test of eating the flowers, to try of they reserobled eggs. This, fortunately, wee not acted upon. Several good microbopic insects were found in the lake. From hence they made their way slowly to the eandetone eaves. The general opinion in the neighbourhood eppeare to be that them naves lave been caused by some mighty natural con- vulsion; but alittle inspection of the outer and inner walls will convince the most eceptical that this notion will not bold water. Mr. John Knowlm traced with ease the pick-marke, both around the entrance and internally, ehowing cunt°. scaly that they have been excavated bv the hand of man , at some time. Mr. Rubinson gated they were reputed to hare been tenantal by the Phoenicians, who had clearly left trace, of their presence all over thie range of hills, as, for example, the actual spot on which they were standing was called the Tent Hill, from the gaideea Tent. Not many years since there were numerous immense granite boulders, with one side slightly excavated. There had hen used an altars in worship. Also, in the field facing the caves, woe a miniature Stonehenge. Some year, Niece, rad to tell, the atonal had all been used for road metal. Inside 'he cave the microscopists gathered some fine tufts of the shining cavern moos, and the fern-like Jungennonnia. The former, when seen with reflected light, has a beautiful emerald green tint, like many miniature diamonds tang over the tavern walls. On a rocky mound, seep well from the caves, he the site of the old gibnet. The last poor fellow suspended here had robbed the post-chaise, on the Chester- road. The chains hang dangling on the came for many years after the body was decayed. On stormy nights, Move the howling winds, the quiet villagers, as they out listening in awe by their firesides, could plainly hear the rattling chains swinging on the hill side., until at length it became unendurable. One man, more courageous than the reat, on • moon light evening carried them and seek Ohs entire lot in Armour's take. After tea, which was heartily enjoyed after this bracing ramble, the party, chiefly under the leaderehip of Mr. Matthews, strolled along Wood- house and Overton Hill., coming out at Dunedale. Takin¢ It altogether this was pronounced the best eecursion of the season. If people only knew what they miss by these healthful Saturday afternoon's rambles, many more would hove joiaed the party. They reached home about nine o'clock, many of them wishing they were going to Hatay again on the coming Saturday. div.p: VOLUNTEER INSPECTION AT ST. HELENS. _ .

The annual impels-Hon of the 4Tth L. R. V. took place on Saturday afternoon, when the corp. assembled on parade at half-past two behind lie Volunteer Hall. The total strength Of the corps i.&18, made up of 90 officers, 43 sergeants, 33 band and bugler., and TOO rank and file. About 850 paraded. The men were pot through a eerier of manual exercise. by Colonel Gamble and the officers; and afterwards the march was commenced headed by the band of the corps to Mrs 'Attlee. field, Denton'. Often. They presented • pretty eight, and a goodly number of spectators turned out to wit- ness the march. A rather laughable incident occurred on the way to the field end which it might net he out of place to mention. As the corpe wee passings certain public house on the way to the fiekl,• few whose cravings ter • drink " was to much for poor humanity to stand, taking into account the enormous strain put upon them by the long 111 dreary much, ran out of the ranks and speedily made to the bar I. anticipation 'of there quenching their thiret. A certain well known pliant major who wan riding close behind, but of whose immediate presence the men were apparently un- aware, P.O spot to his berm and followed the refractory volunteers to the door of the house and demanded their im- mediate return 10th. ranks, a request which was instantly complied with. Having arrived at the field themen weredrawn up in eeparate comp•nina, and afterwards into line. The following officers were present : Lieut.-Colonel Gamble.! Major Pilkington, Maj. Crow, Major and Adjutant Will- I sock., Caplet. Bramwell, Windua, White, Bruner, MeLmr,l Deacon, and Brown Lieutenant. Johnron, Dean, Shade- botham, Garnblg Wareing, Merrieon, Sayer, Cook, Dickens eon, Niel, Hadley, Parr: eurgeon MeNieol. The field is , nicely eituated, and • fair view of the eurrounding district and the enmity chimneys of St. Helens won obtained. AI grand Wand had been provided, and those who went early could swore • comfortable wet on presenting a ticket, but j the salts were so soon occupied that • ticket would hare secured for it. holder nothing more than • very limited imacel in which to contrmt himself or herself. In addition to those on the stand • good 50000 01 the townspeople weembled on i the field to witnees the proceedings. After the lapse of some ten minute. the inspecting officer, Coloeel de Montmorency, commanding tbe 13th and 14th sub-districts, appeared on the scene, and received the usual salute from the colonel and officers, and from the yery long line of volunteere. They I were then put through a variety of evolutions by Colonel . Gamble, and Major Crow, of Widnes. They first of all formed quarter column to the right and marched past in column ; returned in quarter column, and marched post at the double. lb. doable march cannot he ruid to have been well performed, the irregularity of Ho, regiment being painfully apparent. Ti,. manual and firing exercise. were executed with promptnew and accuracy and elicited expreseions of approval from Me inspecting ohicer. Later on they alvanced into line and retired by fours front the right of companies and then moved into square and received imaginary mvalry. Column was again formed, an outward deploy made, and ultimately separam company equates were formed. At 110 clog* of the inspection, the inefxeting officer ex- pressed himeelf plea...ft with the manner in which the majority of the movements bad been gene through, but thought the double might Lye been executed with much more regularity. He considered the condition of the corps reflected credit on the commanding officer and spon all other officers connected with the regiment, but it was some regret to him to tind that the attendance was not no good as that of last year. The books and armour were kept well, and he complimented the corp. upon having good adjutants, to whom exertions the working of • PAlle woo largely due. The CILLIWNIW then gave the tonal Of the day, "The Farnwortb Agricultural Society," coupled with the name of Mr. Whalley. (Hear, hear.) He thought that when he mentioned the name of Mr. Whalley he might be said be I spook of the spinal-morn., of the soniely—(hear, hear),--. ,no that gentlemen was so intimately connected with the show. (Hear, bear.) At the same time he mute not make 1 the name of Mr. Whalley too prominent, as there wore mane !other faithful worken connected with the aociety'a affairs. He believed them was a spirit of rivalry in connection with the whole at the north of England which did not believe in anything which was second rate. He (the speaker) WM in- ' timately connected with the Widnes Athletic Sports, and other eocieties, but he did not know of any of them which were carried on with greater spirit than the Farnsworth Agricultural Society. (Applause.) In going round the I show yard he had seen fine horse, splendid dogs, magnificent poultry, and everythieg in the entrim that wan calculated Ito make each • show memento!. He believed that nowhere in the kingdom was there a show held sway from any great centre of population which woe a better one than that connected with Farnworth. In conclusion, he expremed a hope that the society would continue to grow from year to year in proportion to the great tote and attention given to it. affairs by those who had charge of its interests--tbe spontaneous unpaid labour given to the show by its mcretary, Mr. Hough, its general committee, and all those who mnually supported the gathering by attending there. (Hear, bear, and ap- plause.) Mr. Wnattsr,who was received with applause. responded He said the society hal greatly progressed More he knew it, for he was connected with it when it was in the embryo I state. RA friends hot worked it up to what it wan that day., Ile did not know whether the exhibits they had men there that day earpassed what they had obeerved in years gone by. but he thought they would agree with him that there were a greater number of entries and more stock shown. He I might say that, aa a lomt show, he did not think it WAR sur- passed in the conntry, and he had for many years taken great interest in it. Thera was no doubt in his own mind that agricultural societies had donna great dont of good both to the farmers and the tenant, though he knew that many at his fellow-fanners would not agree with him in this opinion. No doubt the lerdowner had derived more benefit from them than the tenant. He hoped that the some spirit of rimlry which bad in paat years characteriaed the friends of that society would continue to be manifested. (Hear, hear.) Ile thought that the stork, both in cattle and horses. had distinctly improved in that locality Mom the commence- trent of the society's operation, and he hoped they would continue to do no. -7.li;e Climaxaw then delivered the following speech : He said It is with great diffidmee that I occupy the plaid. I do to-day—that of preeident of the important pro. gressive, and enecessfal Farnworth Agricultural Society. It N very well known that I ern not in any way connected with agriculture, and I do not with to occupy your time uselesely, but I will ask your seri.e attention for • short time, for, although I on, not an agriculturist lane raomewhat of a chemiet, and it is from that standpoint I ask you to listen to and reinember what! em going to say. Many , noses may be turned up and many a grunt of disgust may ; be given when limy I am going to speak about that green- , looking, stinking ciinpound, often accompanied by mysterious yellow pools, generally known m" alkali waate." , Before going into the chemistry of this stuff, I think it well do pot one fact about its use before you, beeame fact is stranger than fiction." I know it to be a foot that dieing the winter 1877-78 one thousand tow of alkali waste was carted from the cbemi- cal works at Widnes on to the land in the humediste onigh- boarloood, and used not only ae a manure but as • des•royer of noxious weeds, ground grubs, slag*, germs of dies, kn. I I say destroyer, because the term eradicator would imply the use at impleniento. •nit it accomplishei its inimion. What occurred in the winter of 1978 and 1879? Ten thousand tons of WA. were mated away end put on the land ler the same purpose, and with the same beneficial reauits. 000 gentleman of iny acquaintance, after growing three straw mops on one field. inanured it with fifty tons of waste to the ruatute acre, and grew a splendid crop of potatoes loot year. This year he bas ue that field the fineet crop of wheat or his ion. Not only are the ears full of grain, but the straw lie an strong that it has been able to stand up against the very heavy rains we have had. About a week ago I was !shooting in North Wale, when my friend, who WO, log with inn, mid, looking at an uncut field, What a splen- did crop of scotch gram that would be if it were nut fur the the few stalks of wheat sticking up here ODA tbere among it." Oentlemen, that scotch gnus I could not exist if the field had been properly dressed i with alkali waste—it would have been dead and I

rotten, and actinz urn manure to the wheat. I have no doubt there are many hers who know, but I am wre that there are some here who do not know, and therefore, for the intormation of the few. I ray th,re le an almost inex- haustible eupply of this valuable manure 'mown as alkali- waste to be had in Widnes for the coat of taking it awn. In fact, I May my that I believe Whine* produce. 1,000 tons per day of wame, or shout 300,000 tons per airman. Waste, Co be applied beneficially, requires an much knowledge and forethought as any other strong manure. Where it hoe been must successfully employed, it has been, an early as practicable M the autumn. spread on the land that in going to be plough.' to the thickness of from a quarter to half an inch—h If an inch is about 50 tons to the stetute acre-- allowed to retnaiu expoeed to the action of the air for about • month or six weeks and then ploughed in. The reeult is the destruction of weeds, worms, grubs, Arco and the pro- duction of clean, maimed and without greater cost for labour than ploughing ordinary farmyard manurial land. When waste has been improperly employed, I know there has been a total loss of crop. Bot dm reason is plain. k manure that will kill all noxioun life will kill • seed corn if not properly applied. Waste most be allowed to do im scavenging work before it does its manurial work. Waste does not become a manure till after it has been acted upon by the air, and mug therefore be exposed a eufficient time before being ploughed lido the land. It ie also found that gram crop. after cereals that have been dresseJ with waete are as much benefited as if the land bad received a thorough dressing of lime; but that this should been is only natural, when we remember the chemical constitution of waste. Now, gentle/nen, having put before you plainly, and. I hope intelligibly, the way in which alkali waste rimy most beneficially be used sea manure, I should like to explain chemically why it produces the effects claimed for it. Alkali waste, aa product.' in chemical works. consists of a mixture of sulphide of calcium and lime. The sulphide of calcium in this cmnpound in the most active ingredient. %lien it is spread on the land and expoeed to the action of the air, it in decomposed into sulphate of lime and other compound, of sulphur which are soluble. It is the soluble compoundi of eulphur which tree sink down into theground and du what we may call the scavenging in the land by killing weeds grabs, Sic , not removing their dead b mind, but leaving them to rot and bec3me neefel manure. Neat let on consider the sulphate of lime. Sulphate of lime ie the chemical name of gypapn. I hanlly think I neerl renliu.l farmers that,gypsuin is largely used in the wuth of England an a fertile,, and in France and Belgium it is , eagerly bought by farmers ate price averaging about LAW.; per English ton. Let us go a little further into the considers- , lion of gypeuna and lime as manures. In the researches upon Ode subject commeaced by Baron Liebig, and con- tinued by maily other eminent chemists, it has been found that gypsum has two distinct and important acti•ms as a fertiliser. Firstly, it absorbs ammonia from the atmosphere, and hold, it in • form in which it , can be taken up by plants: secondly, both gypsum aml lime actually dejompose cermin minerals which are abundant in most rails, amongst which I may mention the clay of the Farnworth districts, and not free for the toe of plat. certain materials without which plante cannot live. The minerale I refer to contain anda and potash. Thin soda and this potash are, however, looked op io combination with , silicic sail, and, though slowly set at liberty by the action of the etmosnhere and Mill, and practically unavailable. ..n.l in a form M which they cannot be digested by plants, Gypeum decompmes these minerals and by Pe action sets at liberty their various constituents, and preeents them to the plants in a form in which they non easily be assimilated. Speaking roughly I may ray that the difference between soil dreseed with alkliwaste (that im gypeum and lime) and not so treated is as the difference to as between conkeft and uncooked Meet Besidm the potash and soda thug prepared for assimilation, and which fill the ears of the corn, sillica is set free, and this in the back-bone of the straw, and enablea it to carry the increased weight of the ear uprightly against the Nast of the wind and the downpour of tlie thunderstorm. lient/emen, I have very little more to say, but to chow you that I am not advancing anything new in what I have slid, I must relate to you what occurred mare than forty years urn in the centre of that thoroughly agri- cultural county, Worcestershire. Between forty ana fifty yeare ago my late father (I have shown, I believe, no men ever applied more time, money. or braine to solve the diffi- cult problem of the utiliration of alkali-waste) began Co make soaa in WorceelerShirm. Ile of course prOducerlal waste. Ile used it as manure, and showed the farmers in the neighbouthooel that good crops could fie secured with its. assistance. He told Mem they mould have it if they would cart it away. They would not take it but after a while they wanted it. My father said, “I now want one eh illing a toad for it." From that time the farmers willingly paid the shilling a load, and kept my father's works cleared of waste. Gentlemen. I shall be only ioo delighted If history will repeat itself in this ease, and the farmers of the Widnes dietrict clear the Widnes; works of alkali•warde at a shilling a load. (Cheers.) Mr. Swift ;old there were very strange and material die- Mepanciee in the evidence which bad been given. Crooks, carters in the employ of the Rainford Coal Company, were charged with Malting a ine4 of roll. value lis. 9d.; and Esther Horan, coal dealer, Mareh-street. Liverpool, was charged with feloniously receiving the sante. It Appeared that on the 14th inst. Mottram was aent with a load of coal to • brickfield belonging to Mr. J. Stewart, at Rice-lane, Walton. On the way he met one of Mr. Stewart's employe, who pinned a delivery note for the coal. Instead of taking it there, however, he left it at another kiln, in lieu of a load which Crooks had been sent with, bet which bed he had sold to the female prisoner for 10s. Mr. R. H. Bartlett, who appeared for Mrs. Horan. said she had been in the habit of getting coals from the Itainfonl Coal Company, and that she had no kin but that the coal in question had been sent to her in the usnal way.—The magistrates were of opinion thee the prisoners were equally guißy, and sentenced each of them to a month's imprisonment.
